section_summary: This section documents U.S. investigations into shortages of Chinese silk waste in 1941, emphasizing Japanese control of supplies and possible shipments to Japan or Germany. It then covers a Japanese-backed proposal to barter government-owned raw silk for American petroleum and other commodities, the State Department’s rejection of that proposal, and scrutiny of attorney Raoul E. Desvernine’s role. Later records explain raw-silk trade financing, protest Japan’s discriminatory exporter-quota system, and record the Department of Justice’s post-Pearl Harbor inquiry into the barter negotiations.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on the status of Japan’s silk industry
subfiles.about: The sheet refers researchers to a February 1940 report concerning the condition of Japan’s silk industry.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference from 894.6552 to a paper on Japan's silk industry filed 894.6225/3, with Yokohama officer Boyce.

subfiles.title: Department telegram no. 167 requesting inquiries into disappearing silk waste
subfiles.to: American Consul General, Shanghai; American Consul General, Canton; American Embassy, Peiping
subfiles.about: The Department requests investigation of reports that Japanese firms were taking all available Chinese silk waste, possibly for shipment to Germany.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 167: American Silk Spinning says silk waste vanished from Shanghai and Canton; Japanese buying blamed and a report says waste goes to Germany by Siberian railway; consulates told to investigate.

subfiles.title: Shanghai telegram no. 311 on Japanese control of silk waste
subfiles.about: Lockhart reports on the scarcity, control, and possible destinations of Chinese waste silk.
subfiles.summary: Shanghai 311: Japanese controls make raw and waste silk hard to get from the interior; a Japanese monopoly may withhold or ship waste to Germany; January exports far below 1937, mostly to the US.

subfiles.title: Hamilton letter reporting consular findings to E. John Lownes
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Department of State
subfiles.to: E. John Lownes, Jr., American Silk Spinning Company
subfiles.about: Hamilton summarizes differing Canton and Shanghai explanations for the silk-waste shortage and asks whether procurement problems continue.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton reports Canton blames the end-of-season shortage with new supplies due late April, Shanghai cites Japanese control and possible unrecorded movement; asks whether Lownes still lacks quotations.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 229 asking Shanghai about future silk-waste supplies
subfiles.about: The Department asks whether and when silk waste might become available in Shanghai and in what quantities.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 229 asks Shanghai for concrete estimates of near-term silk-waste supply, timing and quantity for American Silk Spinning.

subfiles.title: Canton telegram no. 14 on seasonal silk-waste scarcity
subfiles.about: Myers attributes Canton’s shortage mainly to the end of the silk season while describing Japanese domination of the market.
subfiles.summary: Canton 14: last season's output about normal, new supplies late April; export needs Japanese approval so Japanese firms displaced others; nearly all waste went to the US, none to Germany.

subfiles.title: Department telegram seeking further Canton supply information
subfiles.to: American Consul General, Canton; repeated to Shanghai and Peiping
subfiles.about: The Department relays company reports of Japanese seizures and asks Canton for estimates of early supplies.
subfiles.summary: Department conveys American Silk Spinning's claim that waste accumulates inland for fear of Japanese seizure or goes via North China to Eastern Europe or Japan, and asks estimates.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with E. John Lownes on silk-waste procurement
subfiles.about: E. John Lownes explains the defense importance of silk waste and reports that Japanese buying has eliminated market offerings in China.
subfiles.summary: Lownes says American spinners cannot buy silk waste at Shanghai or Canton, blames Japanese acquisition, calls it essential for cartridge bags and parachute tape, and repeats the Germany rumor.

subfiles.title: Lownes letter thanking the Department for its assistance
subfiles.from: E. John Lownes, Jr., American Silk Spinning Company
subfiles.about: Lownes thanks Hamilton and Mr. Jones for hearing the company’s difficulties in maintaining Chinese raw-material supplies.
subfiles.summary: Lownes recalls his March 11 meeting with Mr. Jones and trusts the Department will help the company meet emergency needs.

subfiles.title: American Silk Spinning Company letter disputing the Canton report
subfiles.from: E. John Lownes, Jr., American Silk Spinning Company
subfiles.about: The company accepts the Shanghai assessment but challenges Canton’s claim that the shortage is merely seasonal.
subfiles.summary: Lownes disputes the Canton report: inland movement risks Japanese seizure, coastal supplies are Japanese-held and go to Eastern Europe or Japan; asks when American buyers may obtain supplies.

subfiles.title: Hamilton acknowledgment of Lownes’s April 2 letter
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges the company’s renewed complaint and says the Department is again contacting Shanghai and Canton.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton acknowledges Lownes's April 2 letter and promises a further reply after new consular inquiries.

subfiles.title: Hamilton letter summarizing renewed Canton and Shanghai investigations
subfiles.about: Hamilton reports updated estimates of waste-silk production, exports, and Japanese restrictions in Canton and Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton: Canton denies large inland stocks or shipments to Europe or Japan and expects at most 1,000 bales; Shanghai blames Japanese purchases, probably for Germany; the Department will keep seeking ways to ease restrictions.

subfiles.title: Canton telegram no. 19 on silk-waste movements and the 1941 crop
subfiles.about: Myers reports that stocks are negligible, most exports are intended for American firms, and the first 1941 crop will be small.
subfiles.summary: Canton 19: waste silk reaches Canton, exports pass Japanese-controlled agencies, smuggling is risky, no evidence of shipments to Europe or Japan, bales marked for American firms, about 1,000 bales expected after May 1.

subfiles.title: Shanghai telegram no. 431 on probable Japanese purchases for Germany
subfiles.about: Shanghai exporters describe Japanese acquisition of regional silk waste and identify only small prospective supplies.
subfiles.summary: Shanghai 431: six exporters think Japanese buyers take the hinterland's supply for Germany; new waste due late May but export permission uncertain; recent shipments mostly old stock and Chefoo tussah.

subfiles.title: Lownes letter thanking Hamilton for continued efforts
subfiles.from: E. John Lownes, Jr., American Silk Spinning Company
subfiles.about: Lownes expresses appreciation for the Department’s investigation and attention to restrictions on American trade.
subfiles.summary: Lownes thanks Hamilton for his April 23 report and the assurance that practical measures against trade restrictions are being considered.

subfiles.title: Canton telegram on a German-owned waste-silk shipment after the credit freeze
subfiles.about: Myers reports a circuitous Japanese-controlled shipment of Canton waste silk for German owners and eventual export to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Canton: a packer got its first order since Japanese credits were frozen July 26; cargo goes by Japanese transport to Shanghai under Japanese names, then Hong Kong for the US; restrictions raise costs.

subfiles.title: Acheson memorandum on whether to answer Desvernine
subfiles.about: Acheson records Vice President Wallace’s decision that no reply to Desvernine’s silk-barter proposal was necessary.
subfiles.summary: Acheson says he discussed the Desvernine correspondence with Wallace after an Economic Defense Board meeting; Wallace agreed with the Secretary's view and said no reply was needed.

subfiles.title: Desvernine letter proposing a silk-for-commodities barter
subfiles.about: Desvernine proposes exchanging Japanese-government raw silk for American petroleum and other commodities.
subfiles.summary: Desvernine says the Imperial Silk Company holds 37,100 bales of defense-grade silk in Japan, authorized to negotiate through Mitsui, with more available and Japanese shipping both ways, proposing a silk-for-commodities barter to improve relations.

subfiles.title: Barter schedules enclosed with Desvernine’s proposal
subfiles.about: The schedules value 37,100 bales of Japanese silk and list American goods requested in exchange.
subfiles.summary: The silk schedule divides white and yellow 20/22 raw silk by grade and values the total at approximately $14.978 million using U.S. government prices. The proposed American payment included crude oil, gasoline, kerosene, diesel fuels, California cotton, rubber, chemicals, pulp, ink, and other goods valued at about $14.97 million.

subfiles.title: Duggan memorandum forwarding a proposed Wallace reply
subfiles.about: Duggan forwards a draft reply advising that Desvernine’s proposal should not be pursued.
subfiles.summary: Duggan notes the Secretary confidentially conveyed Acheson's assessment to Jouett Shouse, so further discussion is unnecessary, and encloses a draft for Wallace.

subfiles.title: Draft Wallace letter discouraging Desvernine’s project
subfiles.about: The draft tells Desvernine that he should not proceed further with the silk-barter project.
subfiles.summary: Draft Wallace letter: the Secretary of State discussed the matter with Jouett Shouse, and continuing the project would be inadvisable.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Duggan memorandum forwarding a proposed Wallace reply
subfiles.about: This copy repeats Duggan’s recommendation against further discussion of Desvernine’s proposal.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate Duggan memorandum listing the draft reply, Acheson's September 13 memorandum and Desvernine's September 5 letter.

subfiles.title: Duplicate draft Wallace letter discouraging Desvernine’s project
subfiles.about: This copy repeats the proposed instruction that Desvernine abandon the barter project.
subfiles.summary: The draft invokes the Secretary of State’s discussion with Jouett Shouse. It states that proceeding further would be inadvisable.

subfiles.title: Draft acknowledgment to Desvernine, copy 1
subfiles.about: The draft acknowledges Desvernine’s commodity-exchange proposal and says it will be retained for possible future reference.
subfiles.summary: Draft acknowledging Desvernine's September 5 letter and proposing to hold the material in files until action is practical and advisable.

subfiles.title: Draft acknowledgment to Desvernine, copy 2
subfiles.about: This draft copy says the Japanese-American exchange proposal has been filed for possible later consideration.
subfiles.summary: Second draft acknowledgment, nearly identical, avoiding endorsement and postponing action because of complicated factors.

subfiles.title: Draft acknowledgment to Desvernine, copy 3
subfiles.about: A further copy acknowledges and files Desvernine’s proposal without approving negotiations.
subfiles.summary: Third draft: the letter and enclosure remain for reference, leaving only possible future action through appropriate channels.

subfiles.title: Draft letter limiting barter discussions to government representatives, copy 1
subfiles.about: The Department’s revised draft says discussions of the proposed exchange could be conducted, if at all, only by government representatives.
subfiles.summary: Draft says Japanese-American relations have many complicated factors and excludes private negotiation of the barter, limiting discussions to government representatives.

subfiles.title: Draft letter limiting barter discussions to government representatives, copy 2
subfiles.about: This copy repeats the Department’s position that only government representatives could appropriately discuss the proposed exchange.
subfiles.summary: Second draft acknowledges the September 5 letter and effectively rejects Desvernine as private intermediary without ruling on government action.

subfiles.title: Draft letter limiting barter discussions to government representatives, copy 3
subfiles.about: A third copy states that private discussions of the Japanese-American commodity exchange are inappropriate.
subfiles.summary: The language mirrors the drafts on pages 36 and 37. It confines any possible negotiations to official government representatives.

subfiles.title: Duggan memorandum requesting a reply for Wallace’s signature
subfiles.about: Duggan asks Hornbeck to prepare an appropriate response to a letter sent through Vice President Wallace.
subfiles.summary: Duggan says the Vice President forwarded the letter and asks Hornbeck's office to draft a reply for Wallace's signature.

subfiles.title: Handwritten internal note to Mr. Jones
subfiles.about: A largely illegible handwritten note appears to discuss the proposed Desvernine or Shouse transaction.
subfiles.summary: Damaged handwritten note to Mr. Jones apparently asking whether the Department should authorize or support the proposal.

subfiles.title: Handwritten internal query to Mr. Fisher
subfiles.about: An official asks Fisher for ideas on how the Department should handle the matter.
subfiles.summary: Handwritten query to Mr. Fisher calling the problem perplexing and asking for suggestions or whether another unit should act.

subfiles.title: Desvernine letter submitting the barter proposal to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Desvernine sends Hull a copy of the silk-barter memorandum submitted to Vice President Wallace.
subfiles.summary: Desvernine recalls discussing the proposal with Hull and Jouett Shouse two weeks earlier. He says Wallace requested a precise memorandum and that Japanese agencies had since confirmed the schedules with Tokyo. Recognizing the State Department’s policy jurisdiction, he offers to return from New York for further discussion.

subfiles.title: Copy of Desvernine’s letter to Henry Wallace
subfiles.about: This copy repeats Desvernine’s offer of Japanese-government silk in exchange for American commodities.
subfiles.summary: The letter identifies the Imperial Silk Company as the Japanese government’s custodian and Mitsui as its intended representative. It offers 37,100 bales immediately, with additional quantities possible, and proposes Japanese shipping for both legs. Desvernine frames the transaction as a basis for improved bilateral commercial relations.

subfiles.title: Copy of Desvernine’s commodity and silk schedules
subfiles.about: The copied schedules match Japanese silk values with requested American petroleum, cotton, and other commodities.
subfiles.summary: The requested American goods total roughly $14.97 million, dominated by crude oil, gasoline, kerosene, and diesel products. The Japanese side offers 37,100 bales of white and yellow defense-grade silk at approximately $14.978 million.

subfiles.title: Secretary’s office note on communicating Acheson’s memorandum
subfiles.from: Office of the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The note records that the substance of an attached memorandum was conveyed confidentially by telephone.
subfiles.summary: Brief, partly illegible office note documenting confidential oral transmission of Acheson's policy assessment.

subfiles.title: Acheson memorandum opposing Japanese silk imports
subfiles.about: Acheson argues that the United States neither needs Japanese silk nor should permit private barter negotiations designed to circumvent economic pressure on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Acheson memo: Army and Navy said US silk stocks meet two years of military needs; the President withheld silk-import licenses because silk finances Japanese oil purchases; Desvernine's approach is part of a silk-monopoly campaign; stop private negotiations.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Tsutomu Nishiyama
subfiles.about: Acheson records Nishiyama’s representations concerning silk licenses, the Desvernine barter proposal, and payment for licensed Japanese oil purchases.
subfiles.summary: Nishiyama asked the Department to examine blocked silk licenses and admitted consulting Desvernine; Acheson declined a position; Nishiyama explored paying for oil with South American funds, gold or American currency.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on raw-silk distribution and financing in the U.S. market
subfiles.to: Dean Acheson and Department of State officials
subfiles.about: The memorandum explains how documentary drafts, trust receipts, and importer credit financed the American raw-silk trade.
subfiles.summary: The paper describes spot, prompt, and forward sales under the Raw Silk Rules and explains why importers needed unallocated stocks for immediate demand and quality replacements. Overseas suppliers financed shipments through documentary drafts, while American importers relied on ninety-day bank credit and trust receipts before extending up to sixty days’ credit to processors. With approximately 300,000 bales consumed in 1940, the memorandum estimates that at least $10 million in capital was tied up each month. It warns that denying trust-receipt facilities would disrupt importer finance and threaten the entire American silk-processing industry.

subfiles.title: Tokyo despatch on E. Gerli & Company’s exclusion from the exporters’ association
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew transmits correspondence concerning E. Gerli & Company’s request for membership in Japan’s raw-silk exporters’ association.
subfiles.summary: The despatch forwards correspondence between the American Commercial Attaché and the Japanese Foreign Ministry’s Bureau of Commercial Affairs. The enclosed material concerns an American firm’s exclusion from Japan’s raw-silk export-quota system.

subfiles.title: Williams memorandum protesting Japan’s raw-silk export quotas
subfiles.from: Frank S. Williams, American Commercial Attaché
subfiles.to: Bureau of Commercial Affairs, Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Williams protests the absence of American firms from Japan’s raw-silk export quotas and requests an explanation for Gerli’s rejected membership application.
subfiles.summary: Williams protests raw-silk export quotas going overwhelmingly to Japanese firms with none to Americans, argues Gerli merits direct representation, and questions a Yokohama-Kobe minimum-price agreement under antitrust law.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Williams memorandum protesting Japan’s raw-silk export quotas
subfiles.from: Frank S. Williams, American Commercial Attaché
subfiles.to: Bureau of Commercial Affairs, Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: This duplicate again challenges the quota system and Gerli’s exclusion from Japan’s exporters’ association.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate Williams memo: Japanese firms hold 98.84 percent of the quota, American firms none; stresses Gerli's share of the US market and antitrust concerns about fixed minimum prices.

subfiles.title: Raw Silk Export Trade Association explanation of Gerli’s rejection
subfiles.from: Takeo Ito, Raw Silk Export Trade Association
subfiles.about: Ito explains that Gerli lacked exports under its own name and that official policy prohibited admission of new silk exporters.
subfiles.summary: Silk association says quotas reflect five years of exports under each member's name, not nationality; Gerli's exports went through Japanese firms, and its request for a ten-percent allocation was rejected under a ministry ban on new exporters.

subfiles.title: Mizuno letter transmitting the response to Gerli’s complaint
subfiles.from: Itaro Mizuno, Bureau of Commercial Affairs
subfiles.about: Mizuno forwards the Japanese export association’s explanation of why Gerli was not admitted.
subfiles.summary: Mizuno sends the association's reply to Gerli's complaint after the Commercial Attaché's July 10 letter, hoping it answers fully.

subfiles.title: Attorney General’s request for information on Desvernine
subfiles.about: The Attorney General asks whether Desvernine represented the Japanese government and whether his pre-Pearl Harbor barter activities were proper.
subfiles.summary: Attorney General Biddle recalls Desvernine represented Mitsui in talks with State and the RFC before December 7, 1941, and requests evidence on Japanese representation and the Department's opinion.

subfiles.title: Hull reply summarizing the Desvernine barter negotiations
subfiles.about: Hull summarizes the Department’s record of Desvernine’s proposal and offers the full file for Justice Department examination.
subfiles.summary: Hull recounts Desvernine and Shouse's approaches, Wallace's agreement with State's negative view, and Nishiyama's admission that the letters followed consultation with him; offers the full file.
